LESSON · 03 / 03 · BANC V888 SUBGRAPH

A leg moved. What caused it?

This page uses the pinned tibia subgraph to separate three things that are easy to confuse: sensory input, neural motor output, and passive joint mechanics. Run matched conditions, inspect a bounded population trace, and make the causal claim no stronger than the experiment allows.

← Back to the first experiment
Loading reflex-tibia.json…

At the joint sit sensory channels that encode an assumed position, velocity, and limit signal. Their spikes enter this small BANC-derived graph; motor neurons then provide a rate readout for two opposing muscle groups.

The important question is not whether the tibia returns. A passive spring can do that too. Compare the full condition with sensors off, neural output off, and passive mechanics alone. If the motion survives when neural output is disconnected, the motion itself cannot prove a neural reflex.

The model advances in fixed 0.1 ms steps. Every 10 ticks it derives a motor-pool rate, advances the hinge, and records neural torque and passive torque as separate terms. The screen redraws those states; it does not determine the simulation clock.

The extracted wiring is useful for a causal probe, not a complete physiological reflex. Sensory grouping is illustrative, interneurons use generic LIF dynamics, and the passive spring can restore the joint without neural output. Treat differences between matched conditions as model evidence under these assumptions.

Under the hood

The joint angle is encoded, not measured. There is no ruler in the leg. A bank of assumed position channels is tuned across 10° to 150°; velocity channels are direction-opponent; limit channels rise near either stop. Those inputs are sent to a LIF graph with 0.1 ms steps and an approximately 1 ms sensor-to-CNS exchange.

Motor output is read as a 10 ms pool rate. The body then computes two separate terms: neural torque from flexor minus extensor rates, and passive torque from a spring-damper. The plotted angle is the result of their sum. That decomposition is why the counterfactuals matter.

Most interneurons here were not recorded during this exact reflex. Their wiring comes from the extracted graph; their dynamics are a generic LIF approximation, and electrical synapses are not modeled. The sensor-to-motor wiring is measured; the missing physiology is not.

Encoding: Gaussian position tuning, sigma 25°, 150 Hz peak, tiled across 10° to 150°. Velocity: direction-opponent half-wave rectified pairs. Limit detectors ramp inside 15° of either stop. Motor readout: 10 ms boxcar pool rate; neural torque = k(flexor − extensor); passive torque = −kspring(theta − thetarest) − cdamperomega on a single-hinge inertia of 1e-6.

  1. Every interneuron is LIF with generic synapses. Non-spiking interneurons and electrical synapses are absent.
  2. The encoder grid is not the FeCO organ. Functional subtypes are not established by this page's row split.
  3. There is no efference copy, so active-movement reflex gain is not represented.
  4. Pools recruit uniformly here; ordered recruitment is not represented.
  5. Latency claims refer to the simulation clock, not the display refresh rate.
